prompt: Which three factors does OEE multiply?
hint: Stops, speed, scrap.

choices.text: Output, cost per part and number of operators on the shift
choices.why: Cost and staffing are other measures; OEE looks only at the machine's planned time.

choices.text: Availability, performance and quality
choices.why: Right: one factor per loss, stops, slow cycles and scrap.

choices.text: MTBF, MTTR and scrap
choices.why: MTBF and MTTR describe failures over a quarter; they feed maintenance, not the shift's OEE.

choices.text: Hours run, parts made and parts shipped
choices.why: Raw counts are inputs; OEE turns them into three ratios first.

prompt: Another shift: 480 minutes long, a 30-minute planned break and 45 minutes of unplanned stops. What is its availability, in percent to one decimal?
hint: Run time over planned time; the break is not a loss.

prompt: IM-07 lost 63 minutes to stops and 49.5 to slow cycles. Why does the lesson call speed the least visible loss?
hint: What does the floor see when a machine is slow?

choices.text: Because no system records cycle times
choices.why: The controller records every cycle; the loss shows in the count against the ideal.

choices.text: Because speed losses are smaller than scrap losses
choices.why: At 49.5 minutes, the speed loss is far bigger than the 13.5 lost to scrap.

choices.text: Because performance is only computed at the end of the month, when the shift is long forgotten
choices.why: The sheet computes it for one shift; the problem is what people can see, not when it is computed.

choices.text: The machine is running and the light is green, two seconds lost at a time
choices.why: Right: only 1,350 parts against the 1,548 the running time allowed shows it.

prompt: A machine's shift has availability 90%, performance 80% and quality 95%. What is its OEE, in percent to one decimal?
hint: Multiply the three.

prompt: Plant X reports an OEE of 81% and Serra Azul 72%. Plant X counts mould changes as planned stops; Serra Azul counts them as losses. What can be concluded?
hint: Same formula, different inputs.

choices.text: Little, until both plants use the same written definitions
choices.why: Right: each choice moves OEE by points, so the comparison is between two sets of choices.

choices.text: Plant X is nine points more efficient and Serra Azul should copy its methods
choices.why: Counting mould changes as planned lifts plant X's availability by definition, not by any method.

choices.text: Serra Azul is at world class, since 72% is near the usual benchmark
choices.why: The lesson calls the benchmark a rule of thumb, and 72% is not near it anyway.

choices.text: Plant X has fewer breakdowns
choices.why: Nothing in the two figures separates breakdowns from mould changes or speed.

prompt: A machine ran 2,000 hours in a quarter, failed 8 times and spent 20 hours under repair. What is its availability, MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR), in percent to one decimal?
hint: MTBF is 250 hours and MTTR 2.5.

prompt: IM-07 and IM-11 have availabilities of 98.6% and 97.1%. Why does the lesson say a report with availability alone would mislead?
hint: Look at MTBF and MTTR separately.

choices.text: Because availability should be computed from planned time, as in OEE
choices.why: The two availabilities measure different things on purpose; the problem is what one number hides.

choices.text: IM-11 had 15 failures to IM-07's 6, hidden by quick repairs
choices.why: Right: frequent quick repairs are a fault nobody has solved, and each restart scraps parts too.

choices.text: Because 1.5 points is too small a gap for any report to show
choices.why: The gap is small, and that is exactly what makes the machines look alike when they are not.

choices.text: Because IM-11's operators record failures that never happened
choices.why: The lesson's issue with IM-11's log is missing causes, not invented failures.

prompt: The plant manager wants a model that predicts IM-11's failures. What does the lesson say has to happen first?
hint: 9 of 15 failures say "machine stopped".

choices.text: Buy new sensors and train the model on last year's data
choices.why: New sensors have no readings from before past failures, and 60% of those failures have no cause.

choices.text: Switch IM-11 to preventive maintenance on the manufacturer's interval and stop measuring it
choices.why: Preventive maintenance is a reasonable step, but stopping the measurement throws away the history the model needs.

choices.text: Hire a data scientist
choices.why: A data scientist builds the model; without recorded causes there is nothing to build it from.

choices.text: Log each failure with a cause and record the two existing sensors every minute
choices.why: Right: predictive maintenance is bought with history, and the history has to be started.

prompt: When is corrective maintenance, running a part until it fails, the right choice?
hint: Think about what the failure costs.

choices.text: When the plant has no sensors
choices.why: Without sensors, preventive maintenance on a calendar is still available.

choices.text: For a cheap part whose failure stops nothing important
choices.why: Right: then replacing it early costs more than letting it fail.

choices.text: Never; it is a failure of management
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite for cheap, unimportant parts.

choices.text: When the manufacturer gives no interval
choices.why: The plant can set its own interval from its history; a missing manual is not the test.

prompt: A customer received 500,000 lids and returned 90 as defective. How many parts per million is that?
hint: Defective ÷ shipped × 1,000,000.

prompt: Day 12's scrap rate was 3.0%, the second-highest of the month, inside limits of 0.8% and 3.2%. What does the lesson say to do?
hint: What does a point inside the limits mean?

choices.text: Stop the line and adjust the settings before day 13
choices.why: Adjusting for ordinary variation adds variation instead of removing it.

choices.text: Recompute the limits including day 12, so the chart reflects November
choices.why: Limits come from a period known to be stable; mixing in new days defeats that.

choices.text: Nothing beyond watching, since that is ordinary variation
choices.why: Right: the chart answers whether the process changed, and on day 12 it did not.

choices.text: Report it to the customer as a defect
choices.why: Control limits are not the customer's specification; scrap stays inside the plant.

prompt: Which of these statements about IM-07's control chart are right? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where do the limits come from, and what do they answer?

choices.text: The limits were computed from days when the process was known to be stable
choices.why: Right: 25 days in September with no changes.

choices.text: The upper limit is the scrap rate the customer accepts
choices.why: The customer's specification is a separate thing; a stable process can still break it.

choices.text: Day 9 was worth investigating, and a new lot of resin explained it
choices.why: Right: a point outside the limits is a signal of a change.

choices.text: A day inside the limits needs no adjustment, however high it looks
choices.why: Right: inside the limits is what the process does on its own.

prompt: IM-07's shift had quality of 96.0% and first-pass yield of 94.0%. What is the difference made of?
hint: Good, but not the first time.

choices.text: 27 caps that were good only after flash was trimmed off by hand
choices.why: Right: rework costs time that no other number shows.

choices.text: The 14 caps nobody wrote down
choices.why: Those are scrap missing from the shift sheet, a different gap in a different section.

choices.text: The caps the customer returned
choices.why: Returns are counted in ppm, after shipping; first-pass yield is inside the plant.

choices.text: Parts made during the planned break while the team was away
choices.why: The machine does not run during the planned break; that is why it is not a loss.

prompt: The counter says 1,350, the operator's sheet says 40 scrapped, and the warehouse boxed 1,296. Which explanation did Rafael find for the 14-cap gap?
hint: What happens just after a mould change?

choices.text: The warehouse miscounted the boxes
choices.why: The boxes match the counter minus all scrap; the shift sheet is what is short.

choices.text: The machine's counter double-counts some cycles when a breakdown interrupts the shot halfway through
choices.why: The lesson trusts the counter; the gap was traced to what the operator did not write.

choices.text: Start-up scrap after the mould change, binned and not written down
choices.why: Right: the operator wrote the run's scrap and not the restart's.

choices.text: Caps taken as samples by quality
choices.why: Plausible at another plant, but not what the lesson found here.

prompt: Joining IM-11's stop log to the maintenance log, a breakdown appears to be repaired seven minutes before it began. What is the most likely cause, by the lesson?
hint: Three records, three clocks.

choices.text: A technician started the repair before the machine stopped
choices.why: Seven minutes earlier on every event points at a clock, not at a habit.

choices.text: The machine's clock is seven minutes fast
choices.why: Right: the controller keeps its own clock, set when installed and not always since.

choices.text: Daylight saving time moved the ERP's clock by an hour
choices.why: The gap is seven minutes, not an hour.

choices.text: The night shift crossed midnight and the date rolled over in the middle of the repair
choices.why: A date change would move the event by a day, not by seven minutes.

prompt: At Serra Azul, a shift that crosses midnight belongs to the date on which it ___.
hint: The rule at the top of every production report.

prompt: Between the machine counter and the operator's shift sheet, what does the lesson say each should be used for?
hint: What can only a person supply?

choices.text: The sheet for counts, since the operator sees every part
choices.why: A person at the end of a tiring shift misses things a counter does not, such as start-up scrap.

choices.text: The counter for counts; the sheet for the reasons
choices.why: Right: take counts from the machine and ask people for what only people know.

choices.text: Whichever gives the higher quality figure, since both are computed correctly
choices.why: Choosing the flattering one is how the report ends up a point better than the machine every shift.

choices.text: Average the two
choices.why: An average of a complete count and an incomplete one is wrong by half the gap.

prompt: Match each kind of maintenance to when the work is done.
hint: After, on a schedule, on a signal.

pairs.right: When sensor readings say a failure is coming
During the team's break, not counted as a loss

right_distractors: When the customer returns a part

prompt: Put the shift's times in order from the largest to the smallest, as OEE peels the losses off.
hint: Start at 480 minutes and end at the good parts.
items: Planned production time, after the break
Ideal time for all parts made
Ideal time for the good parts only
trap: Taking scrap off before speed mixes the order: performance is measured on all parts made, and quality removes the bad ones last.

prompt: By lesson 17's four questions, what is the typical trap in a factory's data?
hint: The shift sheet.

choices.text: Machines produce too much data to store
choices.why: Volume is a storage question; the lesson's trap is about trust.

choices.text: Every vendor computes OEE its own way
choices.why: Definitions do vary, and the lesson says to write them down; the trap it singles out is a typed number.

choices.text: A typed number sits beside counted ones and looks as solid
choices.why: Right: the scrap column was written by hand and nothing on the screen says so.

choices.text: Machines break down
choices.why: Breakdowns are what the data measures, not a trap in it.

prompt: OEE = availability × performance × ___.
hint: The factor that scrap lowers.
